messages:
maria: just ran an nsys trace on a TRT+vLLM run (8 concurrent streams, dynamic batching). seeing ~30-40% of end-to-end time attributed to our wrapper/scheduler CPU time rather than kernels. attaching a small nsys summary snippet

devon: can you paste the nsys command + the top timeline slice? did you sample or do timeline (sample=none)?

maria: ran: `nsys profile --output=perf/run1 --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=none python -m serve.benchmark --model trt-vllm --concurrency 8`

maria: excerpt from `nsys stats` (trimmed):
```
CUDA API: 24.1%
CUDA CNK: 42.7%
User (CPU) time: 31.8%  <-- scheduler and wrapper stacks
Top CPU symbols:
  scheduler.cpp:enqueue_request()  18.3%
  wrapper/invoke_loop()           10.1%
  kv_cache::lookup_or_prefetch()  2.5%
Top GPU kernels:  compute heavy, expected
```

kyle: odd that enqueue_request is that hot — could be spin-waiting or frequent syncs. grep the trace for `cudaMemcpy`, `cudaEventSynchronize` and `cuStreamSynchronize` and see if they're clustered per invocation.

ashley: also check KV cache hit rates. If prewarm isn't working you might be hitting kvcache misses and forcing many small engine calls which increases scheduler bookkeeping.

maria: quick grep output from the trace: `grep -n "cudaMemcpy\|cudaEventSynchronize\|cuStreamSynchronize" perf/run1.nsys` -> shows repeated cudaMemcpy calls at ~2-3ms intervals aligned with request boundaries.

devon: that points to batching heuristic oscillation — wrappers might be flushing partial batches. what's our batch timeout (ms) and max batch size?

maria: batch_timeout=8ms, max_batch=32, observed average batch size ~3. Using dynamic batching based on token arrival.

tj: try forcing deterministic batching for one run (disable timer flush) and re-run. If wrapper overhead drops significantly then it's the flush path causing extra bookkeeping and cudaMemcpy churn. Also try forcing kernel selector to a single kernel variant (e.g., force fp16-fused) to rule out selection-cost noise.

maria: will do. instrumenting NVTX on scheduler threads to see per-invocation wall time. snippet to add NVTX spans: 
```python
import nvtx
with nvtx.annotate('sched:enqueue', color='green'):
    enqueue_request(req)
```

maria: FYI the CI perf-bot uploaded the raw profile: s3://redwood-perf/perf/run1.nsight (saved)

sre-bot: perf/upload completed: run1.nsight -> s3://redwood-perf/perf/run1.nsight :thumbsup:

kyle: another angle — kernel selection code calls a small benchmark on first usage to pick the best kernel; if that runs on the hot path for many variants it can add CPU time. grep for `kernel_selector::benchmark` occurrences in the trace.

maria: there's exactly one benchmark call at startup only. so not that. I also see `kvcache::prefetch_async()` creating many std::future tasks — possible contention on threadpool that increases enqueue latency.

devon: try increasing threadpool size or batching the prefetch tasks. also capture perf (linux perf) on the scheduler thread to see if it's blocked on futex/lock.

maria: plan: 1) rerun with deterministic batching (flush disabled) 2) NVTX spans for enqueue + kv lookup 3) run linux perf on scheduler thread 4) try threadpool bump and reprofile. I'll post perfetto link when ready.

ashley: sounds good. if you want I can run a synthetic workload that simulates long prefix reuse to stress kvcache warm paths.

maria: thanks — tagging @eng-runtime. will update in this thread with the perfetto timeline and a one-line result (delta in wrapper CPU%).
